questions.question: What does `pwd` tell you?
options: The contents of the current folder
The full path of the folder you are in right now
questions.explanation: `pwd` means print working directory. It prints the full path of the folder you are currently in.

questions.question: What happens if you type `cd` with nothing after it?
options: You go to your home folder (`~`)
Nothing — you need a folder name
questions.explanation: `cd` with no argument takes you home. That is the same place `~` refers to (`/home/yourname` on WSL, `/Users/yourname` on a Mac).

questions.question: Which command creates a new folder named `lab01`?
questions.explanation: `mkdir` (make directory) creates a folder. `touch` creates an empty file, `cat` reads a file, and `ls` lists what is already there.

questions.question: What does `touch notes.txt` do?
options: Creates an empty file named `notes.txt` (or updates its timestamp if it already exists)
questions.explanation: `touch` creates an empty file if it does not exist. It does not open or edit the file.

questions.question: How is `ls -la ~` different from `ls ~`?
options: `ls -la ~` includes hidden files (names starting with `.`) and extra details
`ls -la ~` lists files on your Windows `C:` drive
questions.explanation: The `-l` flag is a detailed listing and `-a` includes hidden files such as `.zshrc` and `.bashrc`. `~` means your home folder.

questions.question: You run `echo "Hello World" >> index.html` twice, then `cat index.html`. What do you see?
options: `Hello World` once (the second command replaced the first)
An error, because `>>` cannot write to an existing file
questions.explanation: `>>` appends. Each `echo` adds another line. `>` (one arrow) would overwrite the file instead.

questions.question: What is the difference between `>` and `>>`?
options: `>` overwrites the whole file; `>>` adds to the end
questions.explanation: `>` replaces the file's contents. `>>` adds onto the end. Both can also create a file if it does not exist yet. There is no undo, so be careful with `>` and `rm`.

questions.question: Which command copies `notes.txt` to a new file named `notes-copy.txt` (leaving `notes.txt` in place)?
questions.explanation: `cp` copies. `mv` would rename or move `notes.txt`, so the original name would be gone.

questions.question: Which command searches the current folder (and folders inside it) for the text `Goodbye`?
questions.explanation: `grep` searches file contents. The `-r` flag means recursive (this folder and its descendants). `./` means the current directory.

questions.question: What is a bash script (a `.sh` file)?
options: A VS Code extension that formats JavaScript
A file that lists shell commands so you can run them together
A backup of your home folder
The same thing as an alias
questions.explanation: A bash script is a text file of commands the shell can run in order. In lab you ran `bash ./start-web-prj.sh`, which created a folder and starter HTML/CSS files. An alias is a one-line shortcut, not a whole list of steps.

questions.question: How do you run a script named `start-web-prj.sh` that is in your current folder?
questions.explanation: `bash ./start-web-prj.sh` asks bash to execute that file. `cat` would only print the script. `open` is for opening files in an app (on a Mac).

questions.question: You want typing `338` to take you to your `csci338` folder. What kind of shortcut is that?
options: An alias in your shell config file
questions.explanation: An alias is a short name for a longer command, such as `alias 338='cd /your/path/to/csci338'`. You add that line to `~/.zshrc` (zsh) or `~/.bashrc` (bash).

questions.question: You added an alias to `~/.zshrc` (or `~/.bashrc`), but `338` does not work yet. What did you probably forget?
questions.explanation: Editing the file saves it on disk, but your current terminal is still using the old settings. `source` reloads the file into this terminal session. Opening a new terminal also loads it.

questions.question: How do you know whether to edit `~/.zshrc` or `~/.bashrc`?
options: Always edit `.zshrc` on Windows and `.bashrc` on a Mac
Run `echo $SHELL` — if it ends with `zsh`, edit `.zshrc`; if it ends with `bash`, edit `.bashrc`
You must edit both or the alias will not work
questions.explanation: This is about your shell, not your OS. Mac often uses zsh; WSL Ubuntu often uses bash. `echo $SHELL` tells you which one you have. Then `source` the same file you edited.
